overview: Ancient brick temple and Buddhist site excavated in the Mahanadi valley.

sections.title: Origins & History
sections.text: Sirpur, on the banks of the Mahanadi River in Mahasamund district, Chhattisgarh, was an important city of ancient Dakshina Kosala, then known as Shripura. It served as the capital of the Sharabhapuriya and later the Panduvamshi rulers from roughly the 5th to the 8th centuries, and flourished as a centre of trade, learning and religion. The Chinese traveller Xuanzang, who visited the region in the 7th century, wrote about the kingdom and its Buddhist presence. The city was lost under mounds of earth for centuries and was largely brought to light in the 2000s by systematic archaeological excavation.

sections.title: Beauty & Atmosphere
sections.text: The beauty of Sirpur lies in its early brick architecture and its quiet, rural setting. The Laxman Temple, built of brick around the 7th century and dedicated to Vishnu, is among the finest brick temples in India, with delicate carved doorways, friezes and ornamental details set in baked clay. It is traditionally linked to Vasata, the mother of King Mahashivagupta Balarjuna. The red brickwork has a warm glow in the afternoon light and illustrates the skill of early craftsmen.

sections.title: Architecture & Highlights
sections.text: Excavations have revealed a rich complex. Buddhist monasteries, including the Anand Prabhu Kuti Vihar and the Swastika Vihar, contain stone and metal images, and the Tivaradeva Mahavihara indicates the importance of Buddhism here. The Surang Tila is a huge temple platform with a series of structures, and the Gandheshwar Temple is an active Shiva shrine on the river bank. The site also uncovered market streets, granaries and workshops, giving a view of daily life in an early Indian city.

sections.title: Famous For
sections.text: Sirpur is famous for the Laxman Temple and as one of India's most significant recently excavated early historic sites, showing the coexistence of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions. It is not yet inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, though it has been proposed for the tentative list, and details of its status should be verified.

visitor_tips: Visitors should plan two to three hours, ideally in the cooler months from October to March.
A small museum shows finds from the excavations.
Raipur is about 80 km away, and Rajim is close by.
